plan.contextChunk: This figure is part of a worked example asking to evaluate the polar double integral of sin theta over the region R in the first quadrant outside the circle r = 2 and inside the cardioid r = 2(1 + cos theta). The figure shows both curves in polar coordinates: the circle r = 2 (blue) centered at the origin and the cardioid r = 2(1 + cos theta) (purple), which extends further to the right. The shaded region R (light blue) lies in the first quadrant between theta = 0 and theta = pi/2, bounded on the inside by the circle and on the outside by the cardioid; a red radial line at an intermediate angle shows a representative radial strip. The figure establishes the geometry of the integration region R needed to set up the polar iterated integral with inner limits from r = 2 to r = 2(1 + cos theta) and outer limits from theta = 0 to theta = pi/2.

interactions.label: Outer polar boundary
interactions.teaches: The formula r = f(theta) determines the outer polar curve, where it meets the fixed circle r = 2, and therefore how large the first-quadrant integration region is

interactions.label: Ray angle theta
interactions.teaches: For each theta between 0 and pi/2, the radial slice runs outward from r = 2 to r = 2(1 + cos theta), which becomes the inner and outer limits of the polar integral

demo_steps.title: Identify the boundaries
demo_steps.narration: The blue circle r = 2 is the inner boundary, and the purple cardioid is the outer boundary in the first quadrant. The shaded region is the part outside the circle but inside the cardioid.

demo_steps.title: Sweep a radial slice
demo_steps.narration: Move theta through the first quadrant. At each angle, the red radial segment starts when it hits the circle at r = 2 and ends when it hits the cardioid at r = 2(1 + cos theta).

demo_steps.title: Reach the intersection
demo_steps.narration: At theta = pi/2, the circle and cardioid meet, so the radial thickness of the region shrinks to zero. This fixes the upper angular limit.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The polar integral comes directly from the radial sweep: 0 <= theta <= pi/2 and 2 <= r <= 2(1 + cos theta).
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Use a clean Cartesian coordinate frame as the polar reference, with thick black axes crossing at the origin. Draw the circle r = 2 in bright blue and the cardioid in purple, with the cardioid tangent/cusped at the origin and extending farther to the right than the circle. Shade only the first-quadrant region between the two curves in translucent light blue. The red radial slice should be a segment, not a full ray: it begins on the blue circle and ends on the purple cardioid. Place math-style labels near the same visual positions as the source: r = 2 on the left of the blue circle, r = 2(1 + cos theta) above the cardioid, theta = pi/2 near the positive y-axis, and theta = 0 near the positive x-axis.
